title: KV Heterogeneous Residency Controller — Playbook for Host Paging & PCIe Backing Stores
content:
Purpose:
This playbook describes an operational and implementation approach for a KV residency controller that manages heterogeneous memory layers: GPU HBM, pinned host memory (GPUDirect), pageable host memory (NUMA-local / NUMA-remote), and device-backed PCIe/NVMe spill. The goal is to keep token-path latency SLOs while minimizing average token cost by leveraging host memory and PCIe backing when GPUs are capacity constrained.

Background and motivation:
- Serving runtime currently keeps most KV state resident in GPU HBM for lowest generation latency. With large context models and multi-tenant workloads we frequently hit HBM limits and must (safely) expand effective capacity without violating tail latency SLOs.
- Existing experiments show PCIe-backed fallbacks reduce cost per token but introduce wide latency variance for first access. We need an adaptive, predictable mechanism that: (1) minimizes frequency of high-latency soft faults, (2) opportunistically prefetches to GPU when possible, (3) uses host memory tiers as middle-ground, and (4) keeps scheduling/capacity policies aware of bandwidth and CPU/PCIe constraints.

Assumptions & environment:
- Linux with kernel >=5.11, userfaultfd available for user-space page fault handling.
- GPUs support GPUDirect / pinned host memory and asynchronous DMA where applicable.
- Server hardware: PCIe Gen4/5 fabric, local NVMe pool for spilling, 2–4 NUMA nodes common.
- Latency SLO: tail (99.9) token latency budget per request is configurable per customer; default target is 150 ms for interactive routes.

High-level design overview:
1) Memory tiers (ordered by latency/cost):
   - Tier 0: GPU HBM (resident, fastest)
   - Tier 1: Pinned host memory (page-locked, available to GPU with GPUDirect async DMA)
   - Tier 2: Pageable host memory (NUMA-local preferred) — can be handled by user-space prefetch and pinned-on-demand
   - Tier 3: Device-backed spill (NVMe/PCIe) — highest latency, used as last-resort spill

2) Residency controller responsibilities:
   - Maintain an LRU-K frequency estimator per key block with compact counters (exponential decay).
   - Keep a dynamic residency budget per model and per-GPU shard that adapts to workload (prefer model QoS targets).
   - Classify keys into hot/warm/cold based on recency, frequency, and upcoming generated token window predictions (see prefetch heuristics).
   - Drive background async prefetch pipelines to move warm keys from Tier 2/3 -> Tier 0/1 as capacity/time allows.
   - Trigger asynchronous spill to Tier 2/3 when residency budgets are reached. Spills should be batched and scheduled respecting PCIe bandwidth quotas.

3) Fault path: userfaultfd-backed soft faults
   - Use userfaultfd to trap page faults on pageable host memory regions mapped into GPU addressable space (or library-managed buffers).
   - On a page fault: immediately try to satisfy from Tier 1 (pinned) pool; if absent, schedule an async pull from NVMe (Tier 3) into a pinned buffer, then DMA into GPU. Return a provisional stall token to request path and record the stall cause in metrics.
   - To bound worst-case latency, implement a fast-path that returns an error/fallback (e.g., synthesize padding or use smaller context variant) if expected completion > SLO budget. This policy is per-route configurable.

4) Prefetch lanes and priority queues:
   - Two async lanes: high-priority lane (can preempt CPU cores and PCIe bandwidth when model latency slack exists) and best-effort lane.
   - High-priority prefetch triggers when the request queue predicts imminent reuse (e.g., next N tokens likely to touch keys). Use a micro-sequencer to prefetch predicted KV indices in order of earliest-needed time.
   - Best-effort lane performs background compaction and consolidates small scattered IOs into larger DMA batches.

5) Eviction strategy: hybrid LRU-K + size-aware compaction
   - Use an LRU-K (K=2) frequency component to avoid thrashing on occasional large keys.
   - Factor in key block size (variable-sized KV shards) when deciding evictions to reduce PCIe IO amplification.
   - Prefer evicting cold but large blocks when bandwidth is constrained; prefer many small evictions when steady-state slack exists.

6) Scheduler integration and quotas:
   - Residency controller exposes per-GPU quotas: max_pcie_bytes_per_sec, max_pinned_pages, pinned_pages_per_model, async_prefetch_concurrency.
   - The serving request scheduler consults these quotas before admitting long-context requests. If admission would violate quotas and SLOs, scheduler can decline, route to smaller-context alternative, or trigger model-variant fallback.
   - Quotas are updated by a Bandwidth Estimator that measures observed PCIe utilization, DMA latency, and CPU steal from prefetch threads.

Telemetry & metrics (must be emitted):
- residency_ratio (HBM_bytes / total_KV_bytes) per-shard, per-model
- page_fault_rate (faults/sec), fault_latency_p50/p95/p99
- pcie_io_bytes/sec, pcie_io_ops/sec, average_dma_batch_size
- eviction_count/sec, avg_eviction_size_bytes
- prefetch_success_rate, prefetch_false_positive_rate (prefetched but not used within window)
- request_stalls_by_cause (host_paging, pcie_spill, prefetch_backlog)

Suggested threshold defaults (starting point for experiments):
- pinned_pages_per_gpu: min(128k pages, HBM_capacity_pages * 0.15) — pinned pool should be modest relative to HBM
- max_pcie_bytes_per_sec per GPU: 10 GiB/s (adjust per PCIe gen & NVMe performance)
- async_prefetch_concurrency: 8 concurrent batches per GPU (tune up for high-bandwidth servers)
- prefetch_window_ms: 12 ms for interactive classes, 200 ms for batch classes
- eviction_ratio_trigger: start evicting when residency_ratio > 0.85 (i.e., HBM nearly full)
These numbers are intentionally conservative; run microbenchmarks per SKU.

Implementation notes and kernel-level interactions:
- userfaultfd: central to predictable soft-fault handling. Keep handlers pinned to dedicated cores; use eventfd notification batching to lower syscall overhead.
- mlock/Pinning: avoid unlimited mlock — use a bounded pinned pool and recycle aggressively. Consider hugepages for pinned pool to reduce TLB pressure.
- NUMA awareness: prefer NUMA-local host pages for pinned buffers; track remote vs local DMA latency and prefer local when prefetching for low-latency routes.
- Cgroup/io throttling: integrate with cgroup v2 io controller to shape NVMe usage and protect co-tenants.

Experiments & validation plan:
1) Synthetic microbench: deterministic access pattern where hot working set fits only when Tier1+2 available. Measure P50/P95/P99 token latency across increasing request concurrency for both prefetch-enabled and disabled cases.
2) PCIe stress test: saturate PCIe bandwidth and ensure quotas throttle prefetch and admission control. Verify that tail latency remains bounded for high-priority routes.
3) Userfaultfd latency breakdown: instrument time spent in userfaultfd handling, pinned allocation, DMA submission, and GPU injection. Target: userfaultfd handling < 1 ms, pinned allocation < 2 ms when pool warmed.
4) Real workload replay: take production trace (anonymized) and run controlled A/B comparing cost/token and tail latency across residency strategies (always-evict, eager-prefetch, adaptive-residency).

Operational playbook (runbooks):
- Detection: Alert when page_fault_rate spikes > 10x baseline or prefetch_false_positive_rate > 30% for 10 minutes.
- Mitigation step 1: Reduce async_prefetch_concurrency by 50% and increase prefetch_window_ms for interactive routes.
- Mitigation step 2: Increase eviction aggressiveness to free pinned pool; if PCIe saturated, disable best-effort lane temporarily.
- Mitigation step 3: If tail latency still violated, use admission control to reject or downscale requests for affected model until backlog drains.

Open questions / tradeoffs:
- How far to push pinned host memory vs complexity of pin/unpin? Larger pinned pools reduce soft-faults but increase system-wide memory pressure and TLB churn.
- userfaultfd vs kernel swap: userfaultfd gives us control but means more engineering complexity and potential deadlock paths when handling many concurrent faults.
- Should we expose per-customer PCIe quotas (enterprise tenants) or keep quotas system-global?

TODOs (short-term):
- Prototype userfaultfd handler + simple pinned pool + async DMA path (owner: Lucas Ortega) — target: prototype by 2025-11-30.
- Build bandwidth estimator module that consumes pcie IO metrics and updates quotas (owner: Maya Singh).
- Test suite: microbench harness and replay runner (owner: Jared Kim).
- Run initial experiments on two hardware SKUs: 8xA100-like, and 4xH100-like.

Appendix: small heuristics checklist for implementers
- Always batch small scattered reads into larger DMA submissions when possible.
- Use LRU-K frequency component to avoid thrashing for large rarely-reused context keys.
- Add a conservative timeout path in userfaultfd handler: if servicing a fault is predicted to exceed SLO, mark the fault as long-tail and signal request scheduler.
- Track per-key last-prefetch-time to compute prefetch_false_positive_rate.
